### Traditional reading (verse by verse)

**v. 1**
- The Hebrew verb for "offended" is the same word as "sin" in 39:9. NET suggests the writer may be contrasting these guilty officials with Joseph, who refused to sin but was jailed anyway. (NET)
- Cupbearer:
  - NET says the post matches an Egyptian official who was often a foreigner and could become the king's confidant with real political power. Nehemiah later held the same job in Persia. (NET)
  - JFB adds that he may also have overseen the royal vineyards and cellars. Both men were high-ranking officials at court. (BH)
- What they did wrong:
  - Gill and the Pulpit Commentary mention an old Jewish tradition (the Targum of Jonathan) that the two men plotted to poison Pharaoh. Pulpit calls this only a guess. Gill thinks it more likely than Rashi's story about a fly in the cup and grit in the bread. (BH)
  - Guzik also thinks a murder plot, perhaps by poison, is likely. (EW)
- Ellicott uses the grape wine in the story to answer critics who said Egypt had no vineyards and so Moses couldn't have written Genesis. He points to ancient Egyptian tomb paintings that show wine-making. (BH)
- Benson says Scripture records this story only because it served Joseph's later rise: the world is governed for the good of the church. (BH)

**vv. 2–3**
- Keil & Delitzsch explain that, as was common in the East, the state prison was part of the same building as the house of the captain of the guard. (BH)

**v. 4**
- "Assigned them to Joseph":
  - Keil & Delitzsch read the Hebrew as "placed beside them" to wait on them, not to guard them. This was out of respect for the prisoners' high rank. (BH)
  - Barnes thinks Joseph had partly won back his master's trust. (BH)
  - Guzik goes further: since Potiphar was the captain of the guard, this kind treatment suggests he never really believed his wife's accusation. (EW)
- "He became their attendant" uses the same Hebrew verb as Joseph serving Potiphar in 39:4. (NET)
- Guzik notes that Joseph used his trusted position to serve others, not to be served. (EW)
- The Hebrew word for these officials normally means "eunuch." Early on, though, it could mean any court official. (NET)

**vv. 5–7**
- "Distraught" (v. 6) translates a rare Hebrew verb, used elsewhere only in Daniel 1:10. It suggests looking sick or worn, here probably from depression. (NET)
- Matthew Henry:
  - It was the dreams, more than the prison, that made the men sad.
  - Joseph's compassion is a model for us, and simply being noticed often comforts people in trouble.
  - We should also look into the causes of our own sorrow. (BH)
- Guzik:
  - A man consumed by bitterness would not have cared about others' faces like this.
  - He compares Joseph to Christ, who entered humanity's prison innocent and never sought our pity. (EW)

**v. 8**
- Matthew Henry says Joseph is careful to give the glory to God. (BH)
- Guzik:
  - Joseph wasn't telling fortunes out of curiosity. He was speaking to troubled men.
  - Guzik lists the many dreams God sent in Scripture and notes that most went to unbelievers.
  - He also warns that not every dream is from God (Eccl. 5:3, 7) and that false prophets use dreams (Deut. 13; Jer. 23).
  - Believers can be open to God speaking unusually, but never against the Bible or on its level. He gives Tertullian's account of a prophetess who submitted her visions to the church leaders to be judged. (EW)
  - Note: you listed Enduring Word among the Pentecostal/charismatic sites. This openness to dreams, kept under Scripture, is the closest thing I found to a tradition-specific emphasis, but I found nothing from another tradition to compare it with.

**vv. 9–11**
- The cupbearer's dream is built on threes: three branches, three stages of growth, three actions. (NET)
- God used images the cupbearer would understand. In the dream he sees himself back at work. (EW)

**vv. 12–13**
- "Lift up your head" is a Hebrew idiom for restoring someone's dignity or office. (NET)
- Guzik:
  - No one could have guessed that three branches meant three days, so the meaning came from God.
  - Joseph boldly gave an interpretation that would be proved right or wrong within three days. (EW)

**vv. 14–15**
- NET's grammar notes:
  - "Remember me" uses a verb form that expresses a strong request, as though Joseph treats the favour as already done.
  - "Mention me" means telling Joseph's story and giving him credit, since Pharaoh had never met him.
  - "Kidnapped" means stolen and carried off, and the Hebrew repeats the verb for emphasis. (NET)
- Matthew Henry:
  - Joseph doesn't blame his brothers or his master and mistress. He simply and mildly states his innocence.
  - When we defend ourselves, we should avoid speaking ill of others. (BH)
- Guzik:
  - Joseph wasn't fatalistic. He took sensible steps to get out.
  - God being with you in a hardship doesn't mean he wants you to stay there forever. (EW)

**vv. 16–17**
- The word translated "white bread" is uncertain. Some read "wicker baskets," and evidence from the ancient city of Ebla suggests "pastries of white flour." (NET)
- The baker spoke up because his companion's interpretation had been good. (EW)

**vv. 18–19**
- Joseph repeats the phrase "lift up your head" from v. 13 but adds "from you." This turns it into a literal, ominous meaning: the baker will be beheaded. (NET)
- Matthew Henry:
  - It wasn't Joseph's fault that he had no better news.
  - Ministers are only interpreters and cannot change the message. (BH)
- Guzik:
  - Joseph delivered judgment as faithfully as good news.
  - He cites Boice's remark that many will preach "the cupbearer's sermon" but not "the baker's." (EW)

**vv. 20–22**
- "Lifted up the heads" is used with a double meaning: restoring the cupbearer and beheading the baker. (NET)
- The dreams came true in every detail. NET says this confirmed both Joseph's gift and his own earlier dreams. (NET)
- Guzik's picture of Christ:
  - Like Joseph, Jesus is the innocent prisoner who shared our condition, brought God's message, and was proved true in three days.
  - The contrast: Joseph's word saved only the innocent man, but Christ rescues the guilty too. (EW)

**v. 23**
- The Hebrew verb form here adds emphasis: he did not remember; he forgot. (NET)
- NET notes the disappointment of two more years in prison. (NET)
- Guzik says God works in both the "steps" and "stops" of a believer's life, and those he uses greatly he first prepares greatly. (EW)
